core_principles.text: The backward lunge is a common alternative to the forward lunge to reduce the quadriceps to hamstrings activation ratio during lower body rehabilitation.
Different variations of the lunge exercise result in different joint angles, which directly impact muscle activity.

specific_findings.text: The quadriceps to hamstrings activation ratio (Q:H) is significantly higher in the forward lunge than the backward lunge.
Kinematic analysis shows a significantly greater knee angle in the forward lunge compared to the backward lunge.

consequences.text: Performing a forward lunge produces a high quadriceps to hamstrings activation ratio, which may be contraindicated during anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rehabilitation.

core_principles.text: The lunge is a unilateral movement that can be useful for identifying weakness in hip and knee musculature that causes movement asymmetries between limbs.
The backward lunge can serve as an alternative to the traditional forward lunge to reduce patellofemoral joint stress and lower quadriceps activation.

specific_findings.text: The traditional lunge exercise can create significant stress to the patellofemoral joint and a high quadriceps-to-hamstrings activation ratio (Q:H).
The backward lunge produces less patellofemoral joint stress and lowers quadriceps activation than the forward lunge.

consequences.text: A high quadriceps-to-hamstrings activation ratio (Q:H) during the traditional lunge leads to anterior shearing stress on the knee joint.

High patellofemoral joint stress during the traditional lunge may be contraindicated for populations needing to minimize joint stress, such as anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rehabilitation patients.

core_principles.text: The traditional lunge is characterized by taking a moderately large step forward so that the thigh of the lead leg is parallel to the ground.
Control the descent during a lunge so that you stop just before the trailing knee contacts the ground.
A traditional lunge utilizes a moderate step that results in the back knee ending at approximately a 90-degree angle.
Performing a forward lunge with a forward lean increases the activity of the biceps femoris when compared to a lunge performed with an upright trunk.

common_mistakes.text: Lunging with a short step length alters the demands on the knee joint.

specific_findings.text: The traditional lunge has a high quadriceps to hamstrings activation ratio (Q:H) of almost 10:1.

Performing a forward lunge with a forward lean increases the activity of the biceps femoris when compared to a lunge performed with an upright trunk, although it does not appear to reduce the Q:H ratio.

consequences.text: A high quadriceps to hamstrings activation ratio (Q:H) in the traditional lunge can increase potential injury risk to the ACL due to high anterior shear forces.

core_principles.text: Using a longer step length during a lunge helps minimize anterior tibial translation over the toes and reduces joint forces.

common_mistakes.text: Using an insufficient step length during the lunge.

specific_findings.text: A lunge with a shorter step length results in joint forces almost two times higher than a lunge with a longer step.
Lunging with the back foot suspended results in almost twice as much activation in the hamstrings, gluteus maximus, and gluteus medius compared to a traditional forward lunge.
Patellofemoral joint loading is higher during the forward lunge when compared to the backward lunge.
Vastus medialis oblique activation and peak ground reaction force are higher during the forward lunge compared to the backward lunge.
Lateral lunges place greater demands on the knee and ankle when compared to the traditional forward lunge.
The study analyzed 34 healthy subjects (21 men, 13 women) aged 18-30 years to evaluate lunge biomechanics.

consequences.text: A short step length causes anterior tibial translation over the toes, which increases joint forces in the knee.
Performing a forward lunge increases patellofemoral joint loading compared to a backward lunge.

core_principles.text: Keep the heel of the front leg on the ground at all times when lunging.
Maintain an upright torso position throughout the lunge movement.

common_mistakes.text: Allowing the heel of the front leg to lift off the ground during the lunge.
Leaning the torso forward instead of maintaining an upright position.

specific_findings.text: The standardized lunge target distance was set to exactly 75% of the participant's dominant leg length.

consequences.text: Allowing the front heel to lift off the ground causes excessive patellofemoral stress.
Failing to maintain an upright torso alters muscle activation patterns during the lunge.

core_principles.text: Forward lunges can be utilized to achieve greater overall quadriceps muscle activation than backward lunges.
Backward lunges can be utilized to achieve a lower quadriceps-to-hamstrings coactivation ratio than forward lunges.

specific_findings.text: In a study of 32 subjects, mean quadriceps activity was significantly higher for the forward lunge at 0.259 mV compared to 0.208 mV for the backward lunge.
The quadriceps-to-hamstrings (Q:H) coactivation ratio was significantly higher in the forward lunge (total mean 6.833) than in the backward lunge (total mean 5.632).
Mean hamstrings activity showed no significant difference between the forward lunge (0.045 mV) and the backward lunge (0.051 mV).

core_principles.text: Forward lunges require greater maximal knee flexion and knee range of motion compared to backward lunges.
Backward lunges involve a greater maximal hip flexion angle compared to forward lunges.

specific_findings.text: Mean maximal hip angle was calculated to be 98.51 (SD = 8.99) degrees for the forward lunge and 102.05 (SD = 8.86) degrees for the backward lunge.
Mean hip range of motion was calculated to be 89.08 (SD = 6.88) degrees for the forward lunge and 90.97 (SD = 7.98) degrees for the backward lunge.
Mean maximal knee angle was calculated to be 116.42 (SD = 6.62) degrees for the forward lunge and 110.29 (SD = 9.23) degrees for the backward lunge.
Mean knee range of motion was calculated to be 105 (SD = 7.28) degrees for the forward lunge and 98.52 (SD = 9.32) degrees for the backward lunge.

core_principles.text: The forward lunge produces higher quadriceps activity and a higher quadriceps-to-hamstring activation ratio compared to the backward lunge.
The forward lunge results in higher patellofemoral joint loading compared to the backward lunge.

specific_findings.text: The forward lunge produced a quadriceps-to-hamstring activation ratio (Q:H) of 6.83, whereas the backward lunge produced a Q:H of 5.63.
Mean knee range of motion was calculated to be 105.42 (SD = 6.71) degrees for the forward lunge and 97.49 (SD = 9.68) degrees for the reverse lunge using a marker-based system.
Mean knee range of motion was calculated to be 97.22 (SD = 5.45) degrees for the forward lunge and 89.62 (SD = 10.48) degrees for the backward lunge using a markerless system.
Performing the forward lunge resulted in approximately 24% higher quadriceps EMG values when compared to the backward lunge.
The group that performed the backward lunge first had a 1.88 mV difference in muscle activation between the forward and backward lunge.

consequences.text: Performing the forward lunge results in higher patellofemoral joint loading compared to the backward lunge, which increases the stress placed on the knee joint.

core_principles.text: Performing a forward lunge results in a higher quadriceps-to-hamstrings activation ratio compared to a backward lunge.
Familiarizing oneself with the bottom position of the lunge can help mitigate instability during the movement.
Increasing quadriceps activation early in the rehabilitation process helps regain patellofemoral joint control.

common_mistakes.text: Performing the backward lunge without prior familiarization can cause instability during the movement.

specific_findings.text: The quadriceps-to-hamstrings (Q:H) activation ratio was found to be 6.83 for the forward lunge and 5.63 for the backward lunge.

consequences.text: A large imbalance in quadriceps and hamstrings coactivation increases the risk of ACL re-injury.

core_principles.text: Altering the torso angle when performing a lunge will change the degree of hip flexion and concurrent muscle activity.
Variations in step length and torso angle can influence joint angles and muscle activity levels during a lunge.
Ensure that you begin in a fully hip and knee extended position at the start of the lunge.

common_mistakes.text: Starting the lunge in a partially flexed hip position rather than a fully extended position.
Altering the torso angle unintentionally, which shifts the biomechanical demands and muscle activation patterns.

specific_findings.text: The forward lunge resulted in a hip angle of 98.51 degrees and a knee angle of 116.42 degrees, whereas the backward lunge resulted in a hip angle of 102.05 degrees and a knee angle of 110.29 degrees.
Knee range of motion was approximately 7 degrees higher in the forward lunge than the backward lunge, which supports increased EMG activity in the quadriceps.

consequences.text: Altering the torso angle changes the degree of hip flexion and concurrent muscle activity, shifting the load distribution.
A smaller knee angle reduces quadriceps muscle activity during the movement.

core_principles.text: Quadriceps activity is significantly higher in the forward lunge than in the backward lunge, resulting in a higher quadriceps-to-hamstrings coactivation ratio.
Hamstrings activity remains similar and does not differ significantly between forward and backward lunges.
Maximal knee joint angles are larger in the forward lunge compared to the backward lunge.
Total hip range of motion is not significantly different between forward and backward lunge variations.

specific_findings.text: Quadriceps activity was significantly higher in the forward lunge than in the backward lunge, leading to a significantly higher quadriceps to hamstrings coactivation ratio.
Maximal knee joint angles were larger in the forward lunge, compared to the backward lunge.
Total hip range of motion was not different between forward and backward lunge types.
